question: When the system needs to tell someone something, does the message reach a person who can act on it — and does acting on it do anything?

findings.title: Every notification badge is inflated, and nothing can ever correct it
findings.method: Recomputed all 196 counter buckets from notification_recipients where read_at is null, matching the trigger's own two-level scheme: a module roll-up stored under sub_section='' plus one row per real sub-section.
findings.why_permanent: The trigger _on_recipient_change is symmetric and correct — increments on insert, decrements on read, re-increments on unread, decrements on delete. The drift did not come from the logic now present, and no reconciliation path exists: no function matching %rebuild%, %reconcile% or %recount%, and no job recomputes the table.
findings.cost: A badge reading 356 against 0 waiting items trains people to ignore badges.

findings.title: 79% of resolvable tickets name an action the executor does not handle

two_distinct_problems.set_quotation_pricing_in_progress: Deliberately removed — the code comment explains it wrote a non-canonical status that normalized back to Draft. Correct decision, but 159 live tickets still carry the string and the UI gives no sign that resolving them is inert.
two_distinct_problems.mark_collection_gl_posted: Appears in no switch case and no grant map, and is explained nowhere. Looks like a gap, not a decision.

compounding_defect.code: const grants = RESOLUTION_ACTION_GRANTS[action]; if (!grants) return true;
compounding_defect.effect: An unrecognised action string skips the permission check entirely and then does nothing. Unknown means both 'allowed' and 'inert'.

findings.title: Accepting an approval ticket changes nothing but a badge

measured.readers_of_approval_result: ThreadDetailPanel only — button visibility, the write-back, and four badge-styling references

findings.note: Live impact today is small; the defect is that a styled comment is presented to the user as an approval.

findings.title: Anyone can post a ticket as anyone, including as the system
findings.effect: An authenticated user can insert a ticket claiming to be from a colleague or system-generated, linked to any record id, and it lands in recipients' inboxes indistinguishable from the real thing — and 97% of real tickets ARE auto-created, so that flag is what a reader would rely on.
findings.contrast: tickets_update is carefully written (creator, or a 'to' participant, or an inbox edit/approve grant plus visibility). The insert side got none of that care.
findings.evidence_note: Confirmed from the policy, the absence of any trigger, and the column defaults. No forged insert was executed against dev — the schema is conclusive and a live probe would have left debris in the inbox.

findings.title: The inbox does not empty — and its read/archive/assign paths have never run
findings.fair_reading: The read path is wired correctly — mark_entity_read and mark_module_read both exist in the database and both are called by useNotifications. The likeliest explanation is seeded data that was never opened, making this a coverage gap rather than a defect.
findings.but: It means the read, archive and assign paths have never been executed by a test, a persona pass or a seed — which is exactly the territory S1's counter drift lives in.

findings.title: The routing engine works, and has two rules
findings.engine: resolveRouting reads active rules by priority, first trigger match wins, returns null when nothing matches so the caller keeps its own default. Rules are data, as the architecture intended.

coverage.unmatched: Brokerage (142) and Trucking (81) e-vouchers fall back to hardcoded default authority

findings.not_a_bug: The engine is switched on for one eighth of the traffic while the doctrine says routing should be declared, not derived.

findings.title: The notification and routing permissions are correct
verified: RLS enabled on all nine tables in this surface.
notification_recipients and notification_counters are strictly self-scoped (user_id = get_my_profile_id()) on both SELECT and UPDATE.
mark_module_read takes a p_user_id argument and is NOT SECURITY DEFINER — which looks like a hole until you notice RLS makes it a no-op against anyone else's rows. That is the right shape.
notification_events is readable only through a recipient row.
routing_rules INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE are all gated on exec_profiling create/edit/delete; only SELECT is open to authenticated users, which is appropriate.

verdict: The plumbing is well built and the permissions are right. What is missing is the far end of every wire: a counter with no reconciler, a resolution action with no handler, an approval with no consequence, an assign modal with no rows.
recommended_order: S2 — 159 tickets that lie about doing something; the `if (!grants) return true` line is a one-word fix
S1 — needs a reconciliation function, worth writing regardless of what caused the drift because nothing else will ever repair the table
S4 — a with_check clause on tickets_insert
S3 — product call: should an approval ticket move the linked record?
S6 — product call: should routing cover the other 92% of bookings?
